name: Kachári
confidence_why: Boro is a tone language in every modern description (Burton-Page 1955, Bhattacharya 1965, Joseph & Burling 2006, Das 2017, Narzary 2019), and Endle 1884's first-syllable stress rule is not upheld: Bhattacharya 1965 treats stress as a concomitant of tone on whichever syllable bears it, and Das 2017 measured no consistent duration or intensity difference between the two syllables of a word.

catalog_quote: 2.—In words where no syllabic accent is used the stress of the voice always rests on the first syllable of a word; e.g., “Faidang” = “fai’dang”; “Faidangman” = “fai’dangman,” &c. This rule holds good even in words where the second (or later) syllable of a word contains a long vowel whilst the first syllable has only a short one, accent being to some extent independent of the quantity of vowel sounds; e.g., “Mosá” (tiger) = “mo’sá,” &c. Exception.—In adjectives beginning with “gă” the second syllable is almost always the accented one; e.g., “Găzá” (red) = “găzá’.” 3.—In words of more than two syllables the accent, as a general rule, rests on the last syllable but one (penultimate). 4.—Nouns in declension— A noun which in its simplest form takes the accent on its first syllable sometimes transfers it to its second when the case endings are appended; e.g., “Mo’sá,” a tiger; “Mosá’ni,” of a tiger, &c. 5.—Verbs for the most part retain their original accent (first syllable) throughout their conjugation; but in compound verbs, the second member of the compound usually takes the accent ... In verbal roots of more than one syllable, the accent almost always falls on the second syllable: e.g., “Ga-glai-nŭ” (to fall) = “ga-glai’-nŭ”; “ge-le-nŭ” (to play) = “ge-le’-nŭ,” &c. Enclitics—“nŭ,” (no,) “sŭi,” (“soi,”)—cause the accent to rest on the syllable immediately preceding them
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Disyllables are stressed on the first syllable and longer words on the penultimate, which together amount to penultimate stress; the examples given for suffixed nouns (Mo'sa ~ Mosa'ni 'of a tiger'), polysyllabic verb roots (ga-glai'-nu 'to fall', ge-le'-nu 'to play') and enclitic-final forms (accent on the syllable before the enclitic) all fall on the penult. Adjectives with the prefix ga- are stressed on the second (final) syllable instead.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Endle p. 6: in long words two accented syllables are marked, a main (double mark) and a secondary (single mark); e.g. Thang'-ni-au''-nu 'even while going' has the main accent on the third syllable and the secondary on the first (the final -nu being 'a kind of enclitic').
new_statements.exceptions: ga- adjectives accent the second syllable (gaza' 'red'); a noun accented on its first syllable may shift the accent to its second when case endings are appended (Mo'sa > Mosa'ni); verbs mostly keep the root accent (first syllable) through conjugation, but in compound verbs the second member takes the accent (khat'-bai vs khat-hing'-bai); verbal roots of more than one syllable accent the second syllable; the enclitics nu and sui put the accent on the syllable immediately preceding them; adjectives in ga- have an ultra-short first vowel (gza, gfut).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement on citation forms and inflected words of Darrang Kachari in 1884, written before tone was recognised in the language; Endle's 'accent' may partly reflect tone. Later phonological work is tonal: Burton-Page 1955 (Gauhati speaker) posits three tones and states that 'intonation and stress are more conveniently considered as abstractions from units longer than the syllable, and are thus excluded in principle from this paper' (p. 341), while noting unstressed, voiceless-vowel initial syllables in words like pi'sa 'son', si'kla 'young girl', ku'ga 'bird's beak' (pp. 336-337); Joseph & Burling 2006 find two tones on monosyllables and could not analyse polysyllables (pp. 17-19); Samy 2011 gives two tones and nothing on stress (p. 521); Das 2017 (abstract) describes Boro as a two-tone language whose lexical tones align to the right edge of a minimal disyllabic prosodic word.
new_statements.identity_note: The only explicit stress-placement statement found is Endle 1884, which describes the Kachari (Bara = Bodo) of District Darrang, Assam, as spoken in the 1880s (Burton-Page 1955 fn. 1 notes that the Darrang dialect 'differs from that recorded here [Gauhati] in several particulars'). Glottolog 5.1 lists only Mech [mech1238] and Chote [chot1240] as dialects of bodo1269; Darrang Kachari has no separate glottocode. Modern standard Bodo is the western (Kokrajhar) variety. All later descriptions (Burton-Page 1955, Joseph & Burling 2006, Samy 2011, Das 2017) treat Boro as a tone language (2-3 tones) and none states a word-stress rule; Burton-Page explicitly excludes stress from his analysis.

new_statements.quote: Results did not reveal any consistent difference between the first and the second syllable in terms of duration or intensity. [...] In Boro, as discussed in 3.1, lexical tone obligatorily shifts to the right edge of a disyllabic domain. This tends to make it appear that the second syllable is specified for stress and for this the tone aligns to it. This hypothesis is obscured by the absence of any durational or intensity difference in the second syllable. Since the most obvious features of a stressed syllable in a tone language are length and intensity (Kidder, 2008), we don’t have enough phonetic evidence in this line to suggest that there exists stress in Boro. [...] Since stress is negligible in Boro, PrWds rely on the contrastive pitch function of tone.

new_statements.relation_note: Endle 1884 (existing statement) puts the stress of the voice on the first syllable of unaccented words; Das 2017 finds no measurable stress on either syllable and, if anything, tonal prominence on the second syllable. Different type (no word stress vs initial stress). Agrees with the catalog that the language is tonal.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Instrumental study of 16 non-derived disyllables (5 speakers x 5 repetitions): no consistent duration or intensity difference between first and second syllable, so no phonetic evidence for word stress; the language is tonal and lexical tone aligns to the right edge (second syllable) of a disyllabic prosodic word, which only makes the second syllable look prominent. Stress is 'negligible'; metrical feet cannot be motivated. At sentence level (5.1.1) prosodic focus likewise shows hardly any f0 or duration difference.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone, not stress, is the word-level prominence: lexical tone obligatorily shifts/spreads to the right edge of the disyllabic domain (section 3.1).
new_statements.identity_note: All opened works describe Bodo/Boro proper (bodo1269), not Dimasa or Kokborok. Endle 1884 = Darrang (eastern) Kachari; Bhattacharya 1965 = the north-west Assam Brahmaputra-valley dialect (northern Goalpara and Kamrup districts), which he contrasts with Endle's Darrang dialect; Das 2017 = Western Boro of Kokrajhar district (Bashbari, Kazigaon, Bhatipara villages), the standard variety per Basumatary 2005; Narzary 2019 = the author's native standard (western) variety around Kokrajhar. Skrefsrud 1889 (not opened) treats Mech of North Bengal/Goalpara, also bodo1269. Work 4 is a review of Bhattacharya's 1977 book, not a description.

new_statements.quote: Three degrees of stress are normally relevant on phonetic level in addition to 'emphasis' or 'emphatic stress' and these are symbolised as 'V, ˌV, V, and "V (strong or loud, medium or secondary, weak and emphatic). In monosyllables or one syllable utterances, strong or loud stress is inherently a simultaneous component to the syllabic tone and as such it is associated with tones /1 2 3/. In disyllabic words or utterances, strong or loud stress either with a medium or a weak stress may be associated with the syllables in tones /0 1/, /1 0/, /2 0/, /0 2/, /3 0/, /0 3/ and the possible (permitted) sequences of /1 2 3/. Emphasis or emphatic stress occurs along with normal strong or loud stress levels in monosyllabic or polysyllabic words associated with relevant tones and one of the contours.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog (tone language with a stress statement). Adds that stress is a correlate of the non-neutral tones and can fall on either syllable of a disyllable; gives no first-syllable default, so it does not confirm Endle's rule 2 (initial stress in words without a 'syllabic accent') but does not name a contrary placement either — Endle's accented syllable and Bhattacharya's toned syllable coincide in being the stressed one. Dialect: north-west Assam (northern Goalpara and Kamrup), explicitly contrasted with Endle's Darrang dialect (Introduction, p. 2-3).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not independent: it is a phonetic concomitant of tone. Loud (strong) stress goes with any of the three non-neutral tones /1 high, 2 mid, 3 low/, weak stress with the neutral tone /0/; in a disyllable the loud-stressed syllable is whichever carries the non-neutral tone, first or second (/1 0/ or /0 1/ etc.), and both syllables can be loud-stressed when both are toned. Three phonetic degrees (loud, medium/secondary, weak) plus emphatic. p. 56 (Tones): 'Vowel-length, stress, voice-quality, presence or absence of glottal check and also pitch register and pitch contour are regarded as attributes to tone'; 'Boro is a tone language with gliding-pitch contour system'. p. 51: '/i e/ contrast in stressed syllables only'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: A 'medium or secondary' degree (ˌV) is recognised; in disyllables a loud stress is paired with a medium or a weak stress depending on the tone sequence; no positional rule for it.
new_statements.exceptions: Emphatic stress is superimposed on normal loud stress in mono- and polysyllables; neutral-toned syllables are weak-stressed with extra-short, often voiceless vowels.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened works describe Bodo/Boro proper (bodo1269), not Dimasa or Kokborok. new_statements.quote: SECTION III.—OF ACCENTUATION. In words of two syllables the penult is generally accented; as obla (then), hajo̤, mountain. But adjectives commencing with g, and words ending with an abrupt semiconsonant make an exception to this rule; as ga-ham (good) bo̤rap' (to be angry), bedo̤r' (flesh, meat). There are also some other exceptions to this rule. In words of three syllables the antepenult generally receives the accent; as hatho̤rkhi, (a star).

new_statements.relation_note: Same default placement as the existing Endle 1884 statement ('the stress of the voice always rests on the first syllable of a word' when no syllabic accent is marked): for 2- and 3-syllable words Skrefsrud's penult/antepenult rule is the first syllable. It adds two explicit exception classes with final accent (ga- adjectives; words with a checked final 'abrupt semiconsonant'), which parallel Endle's marked 'syllabic accent' cases (e.g. gă-zá', mo-sá). It says nothing about tone, so it neither supports nor contradicts the catalog's 'tone language' framing; it is an independent 19th-century description of a different district's variety (Goalpara Mech vs Endle's Darrang Kachari), both bodo1269.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word accent is on the first syllable: the penult of disyllables and the antepenult of trisyllables (both = the initial syllable). Two named exception classes take final accent instead: adjectives with the prefix ga- (ga-hám 'good') and words ending in an 'abrupt semiconsonant' (a finally checked/glottalised consonant or the 'abrupt lenis', e.g. bo̤ráp' 'to be angry', bedó̤r' 'meat'); 'some other exceptions' are acknowledged but not listed. Nothing is said about words of four or more syllables, about secondary accent, or about tone (the work predates tonal analyses of Boro; its word-final 'abrupt semiconsonants.. abruptly checked before they are fully pronounced', p. 4, are the only hint of what later authors treat as tone/glottal check). The word 'stress' on printed p. 76 (Syntax, 'Of words') concerns sentence emphasis and word order only.
new_statements.exceptions: adjectives beginning with g(a)- are accented on the final syllable (ga-hám); words ending in an abrupt (checked) semiconsonant are accented on the final (bo̤ráp', bedó̤r'); 'There are also some other exceptions to this rule' (unspecified).
new_statements.identity_note: Skrefsrud 1889 describes 'the Mech language, as spoken by the Meches in the District of Goalpara, Assam' (p. 1), who 'call themselves \"Boro\"' (Introduction p. ii), i.e. western-Assam Boro/Mech = bodo1269; data from two young Mech speakers over seventeen months at the Santhal Mission, Ebenezer. Endle 1884 (the existing catalog statement) describes Darrang district Kachari; Bhattacharya 1965 the Goalpara/Kamrup (north-west Assam valley) dialect; Das 2017 Kokrajhar (Western) Boro.

tone_statements.citation: Das, Kalyan & Shakuntala Mahanta. 2019. Distribution of lexical tones in Boro. Himalayan Linguistics 17(2).
tone_statements.quote: Boro uses lexical H and L tones and the L is sometimes seen as a default Mid tone (Sarmah 2004). ... The tone bearing unit (TBU) in Boro is the syllable and its tonal organization is such that in disyllabic words only one TBU can bear the lexically distinct tone. ... we conclude that a phonetically rising tone in Boro can be considered a High tone and a phonetically falling tone can be considered a Low tone. ... It is of course out of question that Boro has more than two contrasting tones as word level contrasts were not found to establish these additional tones.
tone_statements.summary: Two lexical tones, High (surface rising) vs Low (falling/low level); one tone per disyllable, right-aligned; toned and toneless affixes, dominant prefixes; F0 data from 5 speakers.

tone_statements.citation: Das, Kalyan & Shakuntala Mahanta. 2019. Intonational phonology of Boro. Glossa: a journal of general linguistics 4(1).
tone_statements.quote: Boro uses lexical H and L tones with the L sometimes seen as a default Mid tone (Sarmah, 2004). These tones can be employed to distinguish lexical meaning of Boro words as in (4) below (Sarmah, 2004): (4a) [ɡáo] ‘tear or split’ (4b) [ɡào] ‘shoot by arrow or gun’ The tone bearing unit (TBU) in Boro is the syllable and the tonal organization is such that in disyllabic words only one TBU can bear the lexically distinct tone. The rightmost TBU is the location for hosting the lexical tone in disyllabic words. ... This study presents evidence for the existence of two tones in Boro: high and low.
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones H vs L (H rising, L falling or low level in f0); one lexical tone per minimal disyllabic prosodic word, right-aligned; toneless suffixes; downstep of successive Hs bounded by the ip.

tone_statements.citation: Das, Kalyan & Shakuntala Mahanta. 2016. Focus marking and pitch register modification in Boro. In Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2016, Boston, 864-868. ISCA.
tone_statements.quote: Boro lexically distinguishes L and H tones [7] as shown below: • gáo ‘tear or split’ • gào ‘shoot by arrow or gun’ The tone bearing unit (TBU) in Boro is the syllable. ... Tonal organization in Boro is such that sometimes only the second syllable may employ the lexically significant tone. While discussing tone assignment in disyllabic words, Sarmah [7] informs that the first syllable in all these cases has the default mid tone and the study also claims that Boro words must have only one tonal specification which is associated with the syllable on the right. The preceding syllable gets a mid tone.
tone_statements.summary: Two lexical tones, H vs L; one tone per word on the rightmost syllable, preceding syllable default mid (after Sarmah 2004). F0 study of focus: H* on emphatic particle and register H/L intonational.

tone_statements.citation: Mahanta, Shakuntala, Kalyan Das & Amalesh Gope. 2016. On the phonetics and phonology of focus marking in Boro. Proceedings of the Annual Meetings on Phonology 3 (AMP 2015). Linguistic Society of America.
tone_statements.quote: Boro lexically distinguishes L and H tones. Monosyllabic words in isolation have two contrasting tone patterns which are phonetically realized as rising and falling. These can be analyzed as underlying H and L respectively (Burling 1959, Sarmah 2004). ... In Boro, distinctive H and L tones appear on the rightmost syllable. ... Additionally, in Boro words, it is not possible to have tones in both syllables. When there is more than one syllable (Boro roots are mostly monosyllabic or disyllabic) the Tone Bearing Unit (TBU) is always the second syllable.
tone_statements.summary: Two underlying level tones, H (surface rising) and L (falling or low level); one tone per word, right-aligned, default mid inserted (Sarmah 2004); postlexical downstepped H; focus markers bear H*.

tone_statements.citation: Sarma, Biren & Jogen Boro. 2015. A critical study of tone in Bodo language. International Journal of Scientific and Research Publications 5(4) (April 2015). ISSN 2250-3153.
tone_statements.quote: 4. It is observed that there are three tones in Bodo language, which is level tone, rising high tone and falling low tone. Level tone: Level tone means the tone level or the level of pitch contour of such words is in level, it seems that there are no major changes of pitch from beginning to end of the sound. ... It is symbolically denoted here [3]. Rising high: Rising high means the tone level or the pitch contour of such words are above the level and the pitch is gradually rise from the beginning to end. Rising high tone is symbolically denoted here [1]. ... Falling low tone is ... [2].
tone_statements.locator: p. 4, section IV 'Result and discussion', point 4
tone_statements.summary: Praat study of 18 monosyllables (2 speakers) concludes three tones: level [3], rising high [1], falling low [2]; reviews Bhattacharya (4), M.R. Boro (4), Chainary (2). No stress remarks.

tone_statements.citation: Burling, Robbins & U. V. Joseph. 2009. Boro tones. In Stephen Morey & Mark Post (eds.), North East Indian Linguistics [Vol. 1], 45-58. New Delhi: Foundation Books (Cambridge University Press India).
tone_statements.quote: Single syllable words that do not terminate in a -p or -t, can take one of two tones. The tone we symbolize as ´ is higher and shorter than `. ... We can interpret tone as a feature of the word rather than of the syllable, so polysyllabic words are analyzed as having just one tone. We recognize each two syllable word has having one of three tone patterns. ... We will refer to the three tones that we recognize as “high,” “low” and “falling”.
tone_statements.locator: draft, section 'Tones of single syllable words' (first two sentences), section 'Two syllable words without suffixes', 2nd-3rd paragraphs (draft has no page numbers)
tone_statements.summary: Monosyllables contrast high (short, often glottal-stopped) vs low; disyllabic bases add a falling tone. Authors opt for 3 word-level tones but say a 2-tone analysis is possible; suffixes toneless.

tone_statements.citation: Joseph, U. V. & Robbins Burling. 2001. Tone correspondences among the Bodo languages. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 24(2): 41-55.
tone_statements.quote: Burton-Page (1955) described Boro as having three tones, and Bhattacharya (1977) proposed four. However, Halvorsrud (1959) allows for just two tones, and this is all that either of us have found to be necessary. ... Joseph ... interpreted the syllables ending in a glottal stop as having a high tone. ... Like Burling and Weidert, Joseph recognized that high and low tones spread, or perhaps move, to the right. Our transcription of Boro words is taken from Joseph’s data rather than Burling’s, so the glottal stops, which in any case disappear whenever another syllable follows, are not marked.
tone_statements.locator: p. 51, section 'BORO'; cf. p. 41-42 'Rabha, Boro, and some dialects of Kokborok are tonal. All of them have a two-way tone contrast' and p. 42 'High tones.. are marked with an acute accent.. The second tone is left unmarked in the Rabha and Boro examples'
tone_statements.summary: Boro: two tones, high vs low; high goes with a final glottal stop that drops before a suffix; tones spread rightward; a lost final -k leaves a high tone (p. 53); contrastive tone position left open.

readall_conflicts: The three readable sources disagree on whether Boro has word stress and where it sits. Endle 1884 (existing statement, Darrang dialect) says the stress of the voice rests on the first syllable in words without a syllabic accent. Bhattacharya 1965 (north-west Assam dialect) makes stress a phonetic concomitant of the non-neutral tones: the loud-stressed syllable is whichever bears tone /1 2 3/, first or second, with no positional default, and lists stress among the 'attributes to tone'. Das 2017 (Western/Kokrajhar Boro, instrumental) finds no consistent duration or intensity difference between the two syllables of disyllables, concludes there is no phonetic evidence for stress and that stress is 'negligible', and notes that lexical tone shifts to the second syllable, which is the opposite edge from Endle's initial stress. Narzary 2019 is silent. So the initial-stress rule in the catalog rests on Endle alone and is not supported by either later description; the modern consensus is tone with no independent word stress.

This rule holds good even in words where the second (or later) syllable of a word contains a long vowel whilst the first syllable has only a short one, accent being to some extent independent of the quantity of vowel sounds; e.g., "Mosa" (tiger) = "mo'sa," &c. Exception.—In adjectives beginning with "ga" the second syllable is almost always the accented one; e.g., "Gaza" (red) = "gaza'." 3.—In words of more than two syllables the accent, as a general rule, rests on the last syllable but one (penultimate).
sources.locator: printed pp. 7-8 (pp. 49-50), 'General Rules relating to Accent, &c.', rules 2-5; secondary-accent remark printed p. 6 (p. 48)
sources.note: Part I §3 Accents, pp. 6-8: stress on the first syllable of disyllables, on the penultimate in longer words; ga- adjectives on the second syllable; enclitics pull accent to the preceding syllable; main vs secondary accent marked in long words.

sources.citation: Das, Kalyan. 2017. Tone and intonation in Boro. PhD thesis, IIT Guwahati (supervisor Shakuntala Mahanta). Shodhganga handle 10603/479240
sources.quote: Results did not reveal any consistent difference between the first and the second syllable in terms of duration or intensity. [...] In Boro, as discussed in 3.1, lexical tone obligatorily shifts to the right edge of a disyllabic domain. This tends to make it appear that the second syllable is specified for stress and for this the tone aligns to it. This hypothesis is obscured by the absence of any durational or intensity difference in the second syllable. Since the most obvious features of a stressed syllable in a tone language are length and intensity (Kidder, 2008), we don’t have enough phonetic evidence in this line to suggest that there exists stress in Boro. [...] Since stress is negligible in Boro, PrWds rely on the contrastive pitch function of tone.
sources.locator: Section 3.2 'Stress in Boro', printed pp. 62-63 = pp. 86-87; also 5.1.1 p. ~183 on sentential stress (Mahanta, Das & Gope 2016)
sources.note: Only instrumental study of Boro word prosody found: two-tone analysis with right-aligned tones in a minimal disyllabic prosodic word; would say directly whether Boro has word stress independent of tone and where prominence sits.

sources.citation: Bhattacharya, Pramod Chandra. 1964/65. A descriptive analysis of the Boro language. PhD thesis, Gauhati University (Shodhganga handle 10603/66710; chapter files 05_chapter.. 12_chapter)
sources.quote: Three degrees of stress are normally relevant on phonetic level in addition to 'emphasis' or 'emphatic stress' and these are symbolised as 'V, ˌV, V, and "V (strong or loud, medium or secondary, weak and emphatic). In monosyllables or one syllable utterances, strong or loud stress is inherently a simultaneous component to the syllabic tone and as such it is associated with tones /1 2 3/. In disyllabic words or utterances, strong or loud stress either with a medium or a weak stress may be associated with the syllables in tones /0 1/, /1 0/, /2 0/, /0 2/, /3 0/, /0 3/ and the possible (permitted) sequences of /1 2 3/. Emphasis or emphatic stress occurs along with normal strong or loud stress levels in monosyllabic or polysyllabic words associated with relevant tones and one of the contours.

sources.quote: SECTION III.—OF ACCENTUATION. In words of two syllables the penult is generally accented; as obla (then), hajo̤, mountain. But adjectives commencing with g, and words ending with an abrupt semiconsonant make an exception to this rule; as ga-ham (good) bo̤rap' (to be angry), bedo̤r' (flesh, meat). There are also some other exceptions to this rule. In words of three syllables the antepenult generally receives the accent; as hatho̤rkhi, (a star).

sources.citation: Das, Kalyan & Shakuntala Mahanta. 2019. Distribution of lexical tones in Boro. Himalayan Linguistics 17(2).
sources.quote: Boro uses lexical H and L tones and the L is sometimes seen as a default Mid tone (Sarmah 2004). ... The tone bearing unit (TBU) in Boro is the syllable and its tonal organization is such that in disyllabic words only one TBU can bear the lexically distinct tone. ... we conclude that a phonetically rising tone in Boro can be considered a High tone and a phonetically falling tone can be considered a Low tone. ... It is of course out of question that Boro has more than two contrasting tones as word level contrasts were not found to establish these additional tones.
sources.note: Two lexical tones, High (surface rising) vs Low (falling/low level); one tone per disyllable, right-aligned; toned and toneless affixes, dominant prefixes; F0 data from 5 speakers.

sources.quote: Boro uses lexical H and L tones with the L sometimes seen as a default Mid tone (Sarmah, 2004). These tones can be employed to distinguish lexical meaning of Boro words as in (4) below (Sarmah, 2004): (4a) [ɡáo] ‘tear or split’ (4b) [ɡào] ‘shoot by arrow or gun’ The tone bearing unit (TBU) in Boro is the syllable and the tonal organization is such that in disyllabic words only one TBU can bear the lexically distinct tone. The rightmost TBU is the location for hosting the lexical tone in disyllabic words. ... This study presents evidence for the existence of two tones in Boro: high and low.
sources.note: Two level tones H vs L (H rising, L falling or low level in f0); one lexical tone per minimal disyllabic prosodic word, right-aligned; toneless suffixes; downstep of successive Hs bounded by the ip.

sources.quote: Boro lexically distinguishes L and H tones [7] as shown below: • gáo ‘tear or split’ • gào ‘shoot by arrow or gun’ The tone bearing unit (TBU) in Boro is the syllable. ... Tonal organization in Boro is such that sometimes only the second syllable may employ the lexically significant tone. While discussing tone assignment in disyllabic words, Sarmah [7] informs that the first syllable in all these cases has the default mid tone and the study also claims that Boro words must have only one tonal specification which is associated with the syllable on the right. The preceding syllable gets a mid tone.
sources.note: Two lexical tones, H vs L; one tone per word on the rightmost syllable, preceding syllable default mid (after Sarmah 2004). F0 study of focus: H* on emphatic particle and register H/L intonational.

sources.citation: Mahanta, Shakuntala, Kalyan Das & Amalesh Gope. 2016. On the phonetics and phonology of focus marking in Boro. Proceedings of the Annual Meetings on Phonology 3 (AMP 2015). Linguistic Society of America.
sources.quote: Boro lexically distinguishes L and H tones. Monosyllabic words in isolation have two contrasting tone patterns which are phonetically realized as rising and falling. These can be analyzed as underlying H and L respectively (Burling 1959, Sarmah 2004). ... In Boro, distinctive H and L tones appear on the rightmost syllable. ... Additionally, in Boro words, it is not possible to have tones in both syllables. When there is more than one syllable (Boro roots are mostly monosyllabic or disyllabic) the Tone Bearing Unit (TBU) is always the second syllable.
sources.note: Two underlying level tones, H (surface rising) and L (falling or low level); one tone per word, right-aligned, default mid inserted (Sarmah 2004); postlexical downstepped H; focus markers bear H*.

sources.citation: Sarma, Biren & Jogen Boro. 2015. A critical study of tone in Bodo language. International Journal of Scientific and Research Publications 5(4) (April 2015). ISSN 2250-3153.
sources.quote: 4. It is observed that there are three tones in Bodo language, which is level tone, rising high tone and falling low tone. Level tone: Level tone means the tone level or the level of pitch contour of such words is in level, it seems that there are no major changes of pitch from beginning to end of the sound. ... It is symbolically denoted here [3]. Rising high: Rising high means the tone level or the pitch contour of such words are above the level and the pitch is gradually rise from the beginning to end. Rising high tone is symbolically denoted here [1]. ... Falling low tone is ... [2].
sources.locator: p. 4, section IV 'Result and discussion', point 4
sources.note: Praat study of 18 monosyllables (2 speakers) concludes three tones: level [3], rising high [1], falling low [2]; reviews Bhattacharya (4), M.R. Boro (4), Chainary (2). No stress remarks.

sources.citation: Burling, Robbins & U. V. Joseph. 2009. Boro tones. In Stephen Morey & Mark Post (eds.), North East Indian Linguistics [Vol. 1], 45-58. New Delhi: Foundation Books (Cambridge University Press India).
sources.quote: Single syllable words that do not terminate in a -p or -t, can take one of two tones. The tone we symbolize as ´ is higher and shorter than `. ... We can interpret tone as a feature of the word rather than of the syllable, so polysyllabic words are analyzed as having just one tone. We recognize each two syllable word has having one of three tone patterns. ... We will refer to the three tones that we recognize as “high,” “low” and “falling”.
sources.locator: draft, section 'Tones of single syllable words' (first two sentences), section 'Two syllable words without suffixes', 2nd-3rd paragraphs (draft has no page numbers)
sources.note: Monosyllables contrast high (short, often glottal-stopped) vs low; disyllabic bases add a falling tone. Authors opt for 3 word-level tones but say a 2-tone analysis is possible; suffixes toneless.

sources.quote: Burton-Page (1955) described Boro as having three tones, and Bhattacharya (1977) proposed four. However, Halvorsrud (1959) allows for just two tones, and this is all that either of us have found to be necessary. ... Joseph ... interpreted the syllables ending in a glottal stop as having a high tone. ... Like Burling and Weidert, Joseph recognized that high and low tones spread, or perhaps move, to the right. Our transcription of Boro words is taken from Joseph’s data rather than Burling’s, so the glottal stops, which in any case disappear whenever another syllable follows, are not marked.
sources.locator: p. 51, section 'BORO'; cf. p. 41-42 'Rabha, Boro, and some dialects of Kokborok are tonal. All of them have a two-way tone contrast' and p. 42 'High tones.. are marked with an acute accent.. The second tone is left unmarked in the Rabha and Boro examples'
sources.note: Boro: two tones, high vs low; high goes with a final glottal stop that drops before a suffix; tones spread rightward; a lost final -k leaves a high tone (p. 53); contrastive tone position left open.
